While the underlying theme—a city-dwelling child returning home to a rural, traditional parent—is a familiar literary trope, the execution here is entirely original and free of clichés. Instead of relying on melodramatic dialogue, stock phrases, or predictable arguments about selling a struggling business, the author uses specific, grounded sensory details (the smell of silt and old iron, the bridge in Dömitz, the cracked plastic cup) and understated actions to convey the characters' complex relationship. Ilse's final action of quietly closing the ferry early to make tea for her exhausted son subverts the cliché of the stubborn, work-obsessed parent and offers a fresh, nuanced resolution.
